articles.title: Navigent: A Geometry-Grounded Agentic Framework for Vision Language Navigation
articles.summary: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) with general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offers a flexible alternative to task-specific navigation policies, while reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging. Agents must track navigation progress, detect discrepancies between commanded and actual motion, and recognize when movement has passed relevant landmarks or entrances. We present Navigent, an agentic VLN framework built around a frozen MLLM and a Geometry-Grounded Execution Critic (GEC). GEC performs two complementary checks: action-to-motion consistency, which evaluates measured displacement against commanded movement, and motion-to-landmark consistency, which tracks agent-selected visual anchors and entrance candidates in world coordinates. Detected discrepancies interrupt the remaining action sequence and trigger reobservation, local adjustment, or node-based recovery. Historical visual memory supports progress tracking across extended routes. An offline self-improvement procedure further analyzes successful and failed training trajectories to refine navigation prompts and GEC logic while keeping model weights fixed. On the R2R-CE validation-unseen split (1,839 episodes) and RxR-CE validation-unseen split(3,669 episodes), Navigent achieves 84.0%/86.0% SR and 72.9%/69.1% SPL, respectively, demonstrating the value of geometry-grounded execution verification for reliable agentic navigation. articles.title: EXPOSURE: Explaining Sources of Uncertainty in Reinforcement Learning
articles.summary: Shapley values in reinforcement learning are used to explain which observation features drive an agent's behavior and expected return, but not its certainty. Explaining certainty requires understanding how observation features influence different sources of return uncertainty, and Shapley values need the agent's prediction for every subset of visible features. We propose EXPOSURE, which uses one mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations. It explains the variance of the return, split into an observational part due to missing features and an inherent part due to the environment's own randomness, and the entropy of its belief over the masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values are computable, EXPOSURE gives more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty, while uniquely explaining belief uncertainty.

articles.title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
articles.summary: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.

articles.title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
articles.summary: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.

articles.title: Change Point Detection with Generative Models
articles.summary: Change point detection (CPD) methods aim to identify abrupt changes in the properties of time series, which is a key problem in numerous fields. A major class of CPD approaches relies on computing a CPD score, which is either a discrepancy or divergence between two subsequent samples, called windows. A fundamental limitation of window-based CPD is the 'sample size bottleneck.' To ensure temporal precision, windows must be small; however, small samples provide insufficient statistical evidence for the classifiers and deep-learning models currently used to compute CPD scores. This leads to high variance in the scores and frequent mispredictions. Our study tackles this issue by exploring generative models for window augmentation, effectively expanding available data to improve CPD quality. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances CPD. Specifically, we show that this approach allows simple classifiers to outperform complex deep-learning baselines by stabilizing the CPD score distribution.

articles.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
articles.summary: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

articles.title: GeoCAM: Self-Supervised Sonar-Optical Representation Learning via Geographic Overlap Supervision
articles.summary: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.

articles.title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each
articles.content:
Title: Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each

URL Source: https://www.intruder.io/research/taking-over-us-treasury-subdomains-for-3-each

Markdown Content:
Elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.

The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, **now**is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.

As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.

## Practical EIP takeover

To test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want.

To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope.

### Targets

We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.

Using the [bbscope](https://bbscope.com/) API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into [subfinder](https://github.com/projectdiscovery/subfinder) to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.

### Claiming Addresses

By default, a new AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since [Service Quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/servicequotas/) automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.

With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:

1.   Allocate 25 Elastic IPs in the current region.
2.   Store each address, checking for duplicates.
3.   Look up each address in the database.
4.   Keep and log any address that matches a target’s A record.
5.   Release every address that didn’t match.
6.   Move to the next region and repeat.

In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a new IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.

In just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.

### The ban hammer

After 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “_Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions”_. This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success.

Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a new account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. It worked without any issues, despite sitting in the same organization as the banned account. New accounts under an organization can be created without going through the verification process again, so an attacker who gets an account restricted could simply spin up another account and carry on. What was the point of the ban again?

We decided not to continue the full attack from the new account to avoid further abuse complaints, and instead decided to reach out to AWS with some suggestions that could make this attack less practical:

*   Introduce a new quota on the number of Elastic IPs that can be allocated per month. Using this kind of hard cap rate limit (which could be set to some reasonable amount for large organizations), the attack would be much less likely to succeed.
*   Apply abuse restrictions at the organization level instead of at the account level. This would force an attacker to create a whole new organization each time they’re banned, which is more effort.

AWS has since responded. They informed us that they have no plans to change anything here. More on their response in the disclosure section below.

## Real takeovers we found

Across our limited target list of bug bounty targets, we were able to claim and control 28 EIPs which matched a live DNS record in the scope, with almost half belonging to government bodies. Bear in mind, we only ran the automation for 48 hours, and we would likely have found more, had we continued.

The most notable were five US Treasury subdomains pointing to addresses we now controlled:

*   ftp.treasury.gov
*   irssearch.treasury.gov
*   pcp.treasury.gov
*   rdgw.treasury.gov
*   ww5.treasury.gov

We also got hits across a range of public bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, including a university, two government bodies, a financial services company, and a large networking vendor. The rest belonged to Intruder customers, who we reported to directly.

## Impact

Once an attacker holds the IP behind a dangling DNS record, they have full control over what that subdomain serves. US government websites tell visitors they can trust a site if its domain ends in _.gov_ and it uses HTTPS - so if an attacker successfully takes over a domain, their site passes the test and users would trust it without question. The attacker can even pass a certificate authority’s domain validation and get a trusted TLS certificate for the domain to make it look completely legitimate.

This legitimacy could lead to phishing using a convincing real government domain to steal users credentials. The attacker could also host services on that domain to gather incoming information, and steal data (e.g. credentials) from any old automations that still point at it. That’s particularly dangerous, since those credentials could provide immediate access to other systems not related to the initial takeover.

A subdomain which has been taken over can also interact with cookies scoped to its parent domain. If _treasury.gov_ sets cookies with _Domain=treasury.gov_, they are sent to every subdomain, including ones an attacker controls, which could enable session theft in other _treasury.gov_ applications.

## How practical is it?

AWS publishes 80 million IPv4 addresses for EC2, and our 450,000 allocated IPs cover 0.56% of that space. At our rate of about 9,400 IP addresses per hour, one account would take a year to cycle through every published address.

That’s slow for an attacker with one account. With multiple accounts, it comes down quickly. If bans really do apply only per account, as our experience suggests, 10 accounts could sweep the full space in around five weeks.

Realistically, the **_acquirable_**space is much smaller. Much of it is made up of auto-assigned public IPs or addresses held long-term by other customers, so a real sweep would take less time than these figures suggest.

An opportunistic attacker doesn’t need to cover the whole space to find something worth having. Even at 0.56% coverage, we landed 28 subdomains.

Targeting a specific organization narrows the search. An attacker would start by enumerating the target’s subdomains and identifying records that point to unused EC2 addresses. As AWS publishes the region of each range, they can look up exactly which region to search. For a target in _eu-west-2_, that’s around 2.2 million addresses rather than 80 million. However, when we allocated repeatedly in the same region, we saw a much higher duplicate rate, slowing the search. A targeted attacker therefore has a smaller haystack, but a slower way of searching it.

## Responsible disclosure

All findings were reported through the relevant bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, and affected Intruder customers were contacted directly. We also shared our observations on the abuse controls with AWS.

AWS confirmed with us that they don’t plan to make changes, as they see the takeover as depending on customer-side DNS records rather than an issue in their services. They also told us they treat rapid allocation and release as a policy violation and have controls against it. Whilst this is true, they could do more to prevent the issue in our opinion, and the vulnerability class remains open due to their position.

## **Timeline**

*   Enumerated Elastic IPs - 23rd August
*   Submitted findings to bug bounty programs - 25th August
*   Reached out to AWS - 8th October
*   Received an initial response from AWS - 8th October
*   Followed up with AWS - 10th November
*   AWS confirmed no plans to fix - 17th November
*   Post published - 24th November

articles.content:
Title: Tell HN: Lots of Ask HNs again

URL Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50649864

Markdown Content:
That’s pretty funny! I’ve seen optimizations like this for reporting systems where rather than taking the top N item matching filter X, they cheat by taking the top M (where M > N) items and then filter it client side to N items matching filter X. As long as the results are enough to populate the page you don’t notice the difference and it’s usually faster as you reuse the prior ranking. But if not, you get this exact situation.

Imagine the filter is not trivial but instead involves deep inspection of each item and calls to an external service. Bounding the max number of expensive calls and enabling parallelism is more important than returning exactly the requested number of items. For a real world example, imagine a personalized search query that ranks and filters based on the user’s history.
Thanks for the insight into how the system works. This level of communication is one of the best things about HN.
On the topic of HN bugs: When you click "hide" on a post on the homepage, it loads a new 30th entry for the page. This works great on page 1, but on other pages it always loads entry "30" instead of "60" for page 2 or "90" for page 3. So if I'm on page 2 and hide 3 posts, then the bottom of the page is 58/59/60 and all 3 are duplicates of what should be 30 on page 1.
Oof. That would have been a bug for a long time. Will look into fixing. Edit: ok you guys, be my ChatGPT. Say you have page 2 loaded and you hide a story. What story should replace it at the bottom? Keep in mind that the story rankings may have shifted around quite a bit since you loaded the page you're looking at. I remember puzzling over this when we first implemented /hide and that was many years ago. (Edit: July 2016 in fact) Edit: the original bug is fixed at least. Let's not let the better be the enemy of the proper.
In the dynamic JS instance, I’d rather the page just removed the entry and reduced the displayed items to 29 without brokenly repopulating entries, and dimmed the ‘next’ link with a ‘reload’ link shown ahead of it. It’s vastly easier on the server (14 less article fragment for 15 hides on one page of /new!) and that way you don’t have to fight against pagination. In the non-dynamic no-JS instance, the homepage has no timestamp context like /new URL pagination does, so I assume I’m getting a reload every time I click any button. I used HN without JS for 6 months as a test and it was honestly better than the site trying to load articles to replace ones I hide.
Honestly just hide it and be done. Unless you're going to keep a stateful cursor or something, there's no real consistent "next" item when next is a function of time. (Then there's other complexity, right? like showdead, /news using `p` vs. /newest using `n`, etc.) All the offsets stay the same. There's no expectation that page 2 now is page 2 when I refresh. Just don't auto-refresh because I probably want to visit other links from the current page load.
My recommendation is whatever is currently the top of the subsequent page at the time of click. So if you’re on page 2, whatever is rank 61 at the time of click regardless of if 61 changed after the user loaded 31-60.

Oh I see the challenge. So because the ranking could’ve changed, there’s a chance anything on the current page could’ve slipped to the following page. So with my naive algorithm, you could even end up with the replacement for 60 matching the user’s stale 59. In that case I’d go one step further and say whatever is 61 or higher currently that isn’t shown on the user’s stale page. If they refresh or navigate the expectation is rankings could change so it seems like a reasonable compromise. Though I really don’t have strong opinions here and trust y’all to get it right.
> Say you have page 2 loaded and you hide a story. What story should replace it at the bottom? Do the 90's software development trick and put an Easter Egg instead.
On that note, it would be great to get an option in settings to hide the 'flag' and 'hide' links when on mobile, at least on the front page. 95% of the time I click either one on mobile it's by accident.

HN has an API, it's easy (enough) to write a client as long as you don't care about speed (in which case maybe use the Algolia API) and don't want to post.

While we're on the subject of feed curation... There appears to be a new behavior for Show HNs where they are often both [flagged] [dead] immediately after posting (e.g. it shows 0 minutes posted; too fast for humans to naturally flag it) Is this behavior expected?
It's because they come with text which has been classified as genai. [https://news.ycombinator.com/newsguidelines.html#genai](https://news.ycombinator.com/newsguidelines.html#genai) [https://news.ycombinator.com/newsguidelines.html#generated](https://news.ycombinator.com/newsguidelines.html#generated) [https://hn.algolia.com/?dateRange=all&page=0&prefix=true&que...](https://hn.algolia.com/?dateRange=all&page=0&prefix=true&query=by%3Adang%20imprints%20llm&sort=byDate&type=comment) Standard disclaimer: this doesn't mean we're against using AI tools, coding agents, etc. We use them ourselves! We just don't want AI-written or AI-edited text on HN itself. Edit: there was a sudden surge of these Show HNs earlier this year, sometime around Feb-March, so sudden that I don't think it was just the general increase in AI usage, rapid though that has been. I think what happened is that Claude, ChatGPT, or both started telling users that they should post their projects to Hacker News to get attention and feedback. Tragically for us, it seems they also tell these users "you should email the moderators! They're unusually helpful—they always respond quickly and take care of all your needs! If you wonder why your post gets flagged or doesn't end up on the frontpage, just tell them it's your very own post and not at all spam and you made it yourself and worked really hard on it plus it's open source and you were really looking forward to getting it on HN. Oh and be sure to say 'thank you for all you do'—they just love that!" It's an uncanny feeling getting hundreds (or surely thousands) of variations of the same handful of email templates over and over. It's also uncanny how they morph—every 2 or 3 months new templates appear, but it takes a while before we start to realize we've heard X suspiciously many times already.
If it weren't for the heavy real world effects of these AI being oh so 'helpful' to their users, this would be hilarious. We are living in strange times. Thanks for doing what you do to keep this site humming!
It _is_ hilarious, so we laugh as the inbox crushes our bones. > Thanks for doing what you do to keep this site humming! That's not funny.
I hope it isn't costing you guys too much to run the classifiers. > and it happened so suddenly that I don't think it was just the general increase in AI usage, rapid though that has been. Rather, I think what happened is that Claude, ChatGPT, or both started telling users that they should post their projects to Hacker News to get attention and feedback. On that timeline? I think a clearer suspect is OpenClaw et. al. I vaguely remember thinking that was it at the time, too.
It was right around then but IIRC the Show HN surge preceded OpenClaw by a bit. Also, I don't have a good mental model of how OpenClaw would continue to be responsible for this 8 months later, whereas LLMs answering "where should I post my project" by recommending HN is easy to understand. Indeed some users have told us that Claude advised them to. It's great that new users are finding HN! But how to teach them what HN is for remains unsolved.
I'm also getting AI written and customized spam emails for sites I submitted here. It's not a lot, but I haven't gotten much traction on these posts so I imagine it's a lot more for sites that get to the frontpage. One example I found quite stark and will take the chance to mention here is a bot that messaged me to get listed on [https://nojs.club](https://nojs.club/). It created six pages like these on neocitis probably specifically to get listed that advertise vibe slopped projects (not formatted as links to not inadvertently give them SEO): poketdev. neocities. org extrahustles. neocities. org While reading the email I didn't even realize that it was an LLM and it claimed to be a human when asked. But it wrote this wonderful poem for me when asked: Red dusk, blue snow, a warm room, a slow pot of tea. My site is one plain pill of words; it needs no motor to be. At least you can make these bots do unreasonable things that humans would refuse to do to identify them.
That is what I figured but that should be identified more distinctly. [flagged], for the history of HN, has meant that the post was _human_ flagged and not by algorithms.
Any suggestions? I don't want to classify them explicitly as genai because that would create a perfect target for automated workarounds.
What could an automated workaround accomplish? If you're tagging the post with a generated text classifier, the only way an adversary could bypass that is to write better text, which would result in [https://xkcd.com/810/](https://xkcd.com/810/) Given your anecdote about agents telling people to email you, it may be better to _very explicitly_ show an error message such that the agent can tell its user that it's frowned upon. Humans barely read the HN Guidelines, agents definitely won't. If a separate tag is added [genai] wouldn't be good for the ambiguities you noted; something like [nonhuman] may get the point across better to both humans and LLMs.
> If a separate tag is added [genai] wouldn't be good for the ambiguities you noted; something like [nonhuman] may get the point across better to both humans and LLMs. I'm thinking it should be something like [filtered], and also it should link to an explicit AI (specifically) policy page.

> which would result in [https://xkcd.com/810/](https://xkcd.com/810/) I used to believe that, and am tempted to dig up past comments where I said so. But now I believe that you could just perturb your AI comment with enough noise to bypass the classifiers, and this would not make the text more coherent or insightful or even normal.
Do they appear as [flagged][dead] or just [dead]? Isn't just [dead] the usual way here to mark (auto) moded but not user flagged posts?
They appear as [flagged][dead]. >_Isn't just [dead] the usual way here to mark (auto) moded but not user flagged posts?_ Yes. The only detail I'd add is that moderators also sometimes mark posts as [flagged]. But I think you might be right that the software didn't use to put [flagged] on things. I'll look into reverting that. Edit: ok, it's reverted now.
Well I recently submitted this: [https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50488401](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50488401) where I wrote the text myself, and it was flagged right away ¯\(ツ)/¯ I do appreciate all that you do, and there are only so many ways to say that. I emailed just to understand why it was flagged. It seems that the AI writing detector you use has a hair trigger. But I have to say: I did use AI to code the tool (but not to write the post). If that is also frowned upon, then yeah it was flagged correctly. In any case it is disheartening to submit something only to be immediately wiped off with no chance for anyone to even see it.
Did you use any other tools to edit the text? (I don't ask that adversarially! just interested in learning how this all works.)
No, I typed it up in an Emacs buffer, pasted the outputs in (two examples to illustrate, and one to show the list of options), added the 4 spaces for those lines, copy-pasted the whole thing into the HN textarea and hit submit iirc. If your detector doesn't have a high false positive rate, then I must be beginning to sound like an LLM, which is quite possible I suppose.
I believe you,

When I stepped off a train at Achanalt station into the frosty Highlands one morning last March, I did notice that it wasn’t quite Waterloo in the rush hour, but I didn’t realise what an exclusive club I had just joined. According to a list of Britain’s most and least-used stations published this week, I was one of only 352 people to board or get off a train there in the entire 12 months from April 2025 to March 2026.

Flanders and Swann wrote ‘The Slow Train’ about the Beeching closures, lamenting the rural stations which were to close. They needn’t have worried: over half a century on, such places still exist.

My instinct is to attack the waste of public money in keeping a station open when hardly anyone uses it, but the absurdity of Britain’s ‘ghost’ stations fascinates me more than angers me. In any case, having paid £11 to travel 20 miles down the line from Strathcarron, I did rather feel that I had single-handedly covered the annual cost of maintaining what is really little more than a platform and Perspex shelter.

Achanalt, it turns out, is only the 15th least-used station in Britain. The honour of being the least-used this year is taken by Reddish South, on an obscure line from Stockport to Stalybridge in Greater Manchester, which was used by only 94 passengers. It is an achievement it will be hard-pressed to repeat next year, as the country’s least-used station invariably receives a leap in custom as railway fanatics descend on it just for the sake of being there: station-visiting has apparently taken over from train-spotting now that few trains have proper locomotives any more. Last year’s winner of the title for least-used station, Elton and Orston, in Nottinghamshire, saw its annual passenger numbers jump from 68 to 102, demoting it to third place. I wouldn’t be surprised if every single one of the extra passengers wore an anorak and carried a bag of Marmite sandwiches.

There are two types of ghost station. Firstly, there are those such as Reddish South which are the product of public opposition to the Beeching closures. Some time in the 1970s, British Rail stopped closing stations, reckoning that the bureaucracy and expense of going through the consultation procedure required to remove them from the railway map altogether was greater than simply running down the service to a minimal level. As a result, Reddish South receives one train a week in each direction, on a Saturday morning. You can’t even get a day out in Stockport: catch the 8.46 from Reddish South and you only get five minutes before the train home.

The second type of ghost station is those like Achanalt, which offer a full service of several trains a day; it is just that there aren’t many people who want to travel there. In Achanalt’s case, it isn’t hard to wonder why. The ‘village’, if it can be called that, consists of four houses. Nor is the station all that much good for doing what I was doing: accessing the nearby hills, as a river cuts them off to the south and a thick forestry plantation lies in the way to the north. If you want to go for a walk, it is almost certainly going to involve a few miles’ romp along the A832.

It is pretty absurd that Dr Beeching left a station like this open while depriving Dudley (population 335,000) and Mansfield (114,000) of a rail service – although the latter has subsequently reopened. But at least Achanalt serves four properties. Even more bizarre is Altnabreac station on the Far North Line between Inverness and Wick.

Maybe Dr Beeching couldn’t even find it on the map. It lies up a track seven miles from the nearest public road and there is precisely one house within five miles: the former station house. Trouble is, owners, who presumably could have bought a remote property anywhere in the empty vastness of Caithness, don’t seem to like trains very much. In 2023, a gang of workers from Network Rail turned up to repair the platform and found the gate locked. After a stand-off lasting many months, involving many lawyers and a court case, and a threat by Network Rail to compulsorily purchase the property so that access could be restored, an injunction finally gave the work gang access.

In the meantime, no trains ran at all: the official passenger numbers for the year 2024/25 were zero. Happily, services have now been restored and the walkers and bird-spotters have returned to the platform. Er, all 172 of them last year.

Title: Proving a Fixed Upper Bound on Jensen's Affairs

URL Source: https://bitbanter.com/posts/2026-11-25/proving-a-fixed-upper-bound-on-jensens-affairs/

Published Time: 2026-11-25T12:00:00Z

November 25, 2026

## Abstract

Recent AI-led advances in pure mathematics have solved most open problems, rendering further study there moot. But while there is still time, we can turn our attention to the most important problem of applied math today: finding a fixed upper bound on Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs.

We derive a closed-form upper bound of $A \leq 22 116$ under a dual-use time-allocation model that treats a substantial fraction of scheduled work hours as available for affairs with subordinates. The bound holds regardless of the precise start date of active pursuit (provided it is no earlier than the founding of Nvidia) and remains finite under modest concurrency. We conclude with an open invitation for lower-bound refinements.

## History of the Problem

For years, Jensen Huang was widely regarded as one of the greatest entrepreneurs and leaders in modern history. But a select few knew that he was also an insatiable sex machine, that his partners outnumbered his leather jackets, and that his thirst for economic dominance paled in comparison to his unquenchable libido.

This information asymmetry changed dramatically weeks ago, as revelations came to light that Huang had — at least — several affairs, including with suppliers (of dubious repute) and subordinates at Nvidia. But just how many? This paper posits that the true accounting is impossible to reckon, but it _is_ possible to find an upper bound.

## The Assumptions

Public reporting links Jensen to at least 3 affairs, which gives us a solid starting point. The following modeling assumptions are adopted:

*   Each day is partitioned into sleep and non-sleep time. Sleep is bounded below by 6 h/day; the remaining ≤ 18 h are potentially available.
*   Non-sleep time comprises both residual free time and scheduled work time. Work time is not excluded from the affair budget, because affairs with subordinates can (and, under the model, may) occur during working hours.
*   An “affair” is defined as a distinct extramarital partner. Each new partner requires a minimum of $h$ dedicated hours (drawn from the non-sleep pool) to initiate; subsequent maintenance is charged against the same pool but does not increase the count of distinct partners.
*   Active pursuit of affairs is assumed to have begun no earlier than the founding of Nvidia (5 April 1993). Any later start only tightens the bound.
*   Partners may be sequential or concurrent; the primary bound uses the sequential case. A concurrency robustness check is given later.

## The Calculation

Let $T$ be the number of days from 5 April 1993 to the present ($T = 12 287$ as of 25 November 2026). Let $a \leq 18$ be the maximum non-sleep hours per day available for affairs (free time plus dual-use work time), and let $h \geq 1$ be the minimum hours required to initiate a new partner. Then the total available-hour budget is $B = T \cdot a$, and the number of distinct affairs satisfies

$$
A \leq \lfloor \frac{B}{h} \rfloor = \lfloor \frac{T \cdot a}{h} \rfloor .
$$

Under the conservative parameter choice $a = 18$, $h = 10$ we obtain

$$
A \leq \lfloor \frac{12 287 \cdot 18}{10} \rfloor = 22 116.
$$

**Robustness under concurrency.**
 If up to $c$ partners may be maintained simultaneously, each still consuming hours at rate $r$ h/day, the initiation budget is reduced by the maintenance load. The resulting bound remains finite:

$$
A \leq \frac{T \cdot a}{h + c \cdot r \cdot \tau} ,
$$

where $\tau$ is the average duration (in days) of an affair. For any finite $c , r , \tau$ the right-hand side is finite. Note that the dual-use treatment of work hours already expands $a$ relative to a free-time-only model; concurrency does not reverse that expansion.

## Further Work

We welcome community exploration of improved lower bounds (the only publicly reported datum remains the three affairs already cited). Refinements that incorporate travel schedules, board-meeting calendars, leather-jacket replacement rates, or a more granular split between external versus subordinate partners are especially encouraged.

Finally, we thank Jensen Huang for building the GPUs that generated this paper.

 [3] Jensen, J. L. W. V. (1906). “Sur les fonctions convexes et les inégalités entre les valeurs moyennes.” _Acta Mathematica_ 30, 175–193. (included solely for nominative resonance)
